summary: L-Glutamate (L-glutamic acid) is a non-essential amino acid that is the most abundant free amino acid in the body and the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. Metabolically it is a hub for transamination and nitrogen transfer and a precursor for glutamine, glutathione, and (via decarboxylation) GABA. It is consumed as a dietary protein constituent and sold as an amino-acid dietary supplement; the hydrochloride salt has historically been used as an oral gastric acidifier in hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria. IMPORTANT: it is an amino acid/supplement and NOT an FDA-approved drug, so there is no single FDA label and dosing/indications derive from monographs and the older pharmaceutical literature. Orally ingested glutamate is largely metabolized by the gut and does not freely cross the blood-brain barrier, so dietary intake does not directly raise brain neurotransmitter levels.

moa: L-Glutamate is a non-essential amino acid central to nitrogen metabolism and neurotransmission. It is the major excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system, acting on ionotropic (NMDA, AMPA, kainate) and metabotropic glutamate receptors; however, dietary/oral glutamate is extensively metabolized by enterocytes and does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so oral intake does not directly augment central neurotransmission. Metabolically, glutamate is the principal amino group acceptor/donor in transamination reactions (interconverting with alpha-ketoglutarate in the Krebs cycle), the immediate precursor of glutamine (via glutamine synthetase), of the inhibitory transmitter GABA (via glutamate decarboxylase), and a constituent of the antioxidant glutathione. As the hydrochloride salt it liberates hydrochloric acid in the stomach, transiently lowering gastric pH - the rationale for its historical use as a gastric acidifier.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to glutamic acid or product components
Glutamic acid hydrochloride is contraindicated where gastric acidification is harmful (e.g., active peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, gastroesophageal reflux, hyperchlorhydria)
relative: Individuals reporting sensitivity to glutamate (headache, flushing, palpitations)
monitor: Generally none for ordinary dietary use
Gastrointestinal symptoms with the acidifier salt
Biochemical parameters only in specific supervised clinical contexts

preg: Glutamic acid is a naturally abundant dietary amino acid, and ordinary dietary intake is considered low risk in pregnancy. There are no adequate data supporting high-dose supplemental use during pregnancy; reserve supplementation beyond dietary amounts for clear clinical indications under supervision.
lact: Glutamate is naturally present in human milk and in the diet. There are limited data on high-dose supplementation during breastfeeding; supplemental use beyond normal dietary intake should be supervised.
renal: No specific dosing data; use caution with large amino-acid/nitrogen loads in significant renal impairment, where handling of a nitrogen load is reduced.
hepatic: No specific dosing data; use caution in severe hepatic impairment because the liver is central to glutamate/glutamine and nitrogen metabolism.

minor: Antacids and acid-suppressing drugs (proton-pump inhibitors, H2 blockers) - oppose the gastric-acidifying effect of glutamic acid hydrochloride
Other amino-acid supplements (theoretical competition for intestinal transport)
interactions.food: Take with food/meals; dietary protein is a major natural source of glutamate.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described; general moderation advised.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference at dietary intake; isolated high loads could transiently affect amino-acid/ammonia panels.

common: Generally well tolerated at dietary amounts
Mild gastrointestinal upset, nausea, or fullness with the hydrochloride salt or large doses
serious: No well-documented serious adverse effects from oral supplemental glutamate in usual amounts
rare: Self-reported symptom complex in sensitive individuals (headache, flushing, sweating, palpitations - the so-called 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' attributed to glutamate)

Gastrointestinal tolerance when used as a gastric acidifier salt

counsel: This is a naturally occurring amino acid sold as a dietary supplement; it is not an FDA-approved medicine
Take it with food to reduce stomach upset
Do not use the acid (hydrochloride) form if you have heartburn, reflux, gastritis, or an ulcer
Eating glutamate by mouth does not directly raise the level of this chemical in your brain - it is broken down in the gut
Tell your clinician about all supplements you take, especially if you have kidney or liver problems
pk: Absorbed and metabolized over minutes to hours; largely used by the intestinal mucosa
Plasma amino-acid peak roughly 0.5-2 hours after an oral dose; mostly buffered by gut metabolism
Short - rapidly transaminated/metabolized; not a fixed pharmacologic half-life
Transient; incorporated into metabolic pools rather than producing a sustained drug effect
Store at room temperature, tightly closed, protected from moisture
pearls: DIETARY SUPPLEMENT / amino acid - NOT an FDA-approved drug; data drawn from monographs and older pharmaceutical literature (e.g., glutamic acid hydrochloride as a gastric acidifier) rather than an FDA label
Most abundant free amino acid and the principal excitatory CNS neurotransmitter - but oral glutamate is gut-metabolized and does NOT freely cross the blood-brain barrier
The hydrochloride salt was historically used to acidify gastric contents in achlorhydria/hypochlorhydria - avoid in reflux/ulcer/hyperacidity
Generally well tolerated at dietary amounts; no robust evidence for cognitive or performance 'nootropic' claims
Be conservative: no established therapeutic single-supplement indication or standardized dose
missed: If you miss a dose of an oral supplement, take it when you remember, or skip it if it is nearly time for the next dose; do not double up. There is no need to compensate for a missed dose of a dietary amino acid.
overdose: Acute overdose of oral glutamate is expected to cause, at most, self-limited gastrointestinal upset and possibly headache or flushing in sensitive individuals; there is no specific antidote and management is supportive with hydration. Very large isolated amino-acid/nitrogen loads should be avoided in renal or hepatic impairment.
